extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, translators and practitioners of classical poetics and drama (playwrights, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of Aristotle's Poetics (Latin & Greek, with editorial notes) giving prescriptive and evaluative principles for composing and judging epic poetry and tragedy—covering plot, character, devices, length, and performance constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Plot must be a single complete action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should imitate a single action that is whole and complete, having a beginning, middle, and end; the plot should form a cohesive, contiguous process rather than a mere sequence of loosely related episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly emphasizes a complete, ordered action as the primary constituent of tragedy: avoid digressions that would make the argument or sequence fall apart; ornamentation of the argument should not mask a defect in the plot's unity. Use peripeteia (reversal) and anagnorisis (recognition) as structural devices within this single action to produce the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Appropriate Length
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must have an appropriate magnitude: not too short to be trivial nor too long to lose unity and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle notes that tragedies as performed should occupy a limited time (see unity of time), and that an epic (epopeia) must not be made larger than the aggregate amount of tragedy comfortably heard in a single day: 'Spectandum Aristoteles tradit tempus... uno die'—epic authors should gauge length against the total of tragedies recited in that one day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character: appropriateness, consistency, and fit to action
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be plausible, consistent with their natures, and appropriate to the plot's requirements; the poet 'should imitate angry and furious persons' when the action requires such passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary states: 'Poetam oportet qui iracundos & furibundes, & tales PerSonas imitetur' — choose characters whose dispositions (noble, base, furious, etc.) suit the deeds they perform; avoid characters acting against their established nature unless the plot provides convincing motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and Necessity (Verisimilitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot should arise from probability or necessity rather than pure chance; the sequence of cause and effect must appear plausible to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle contrasts what is probable/necessary with what is accidental; plots should be constructed so that outcomes follow from preceding circumstances and character, thereby maintaining verisimilitude and moral/causal intelligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (Eliciting pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy's purpose is to arouse pity and fear in the audience and to effect a purgation (catharsis) of these emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although phrasing and extended commentary vary, the text treats the evocation and transformation of audience emotions as a central evaluative aim—plot, character, and devices should be marshalled to produce that emotional outcome rather than spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal) and Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use reversals of fortune and recognitions (discoveries) as key devices to produce tragic effects; their interplay can produce the most powerful emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes explain recognition often proceeds from what seems like a plausible but false reasoning by the spectator and cite examples (e.g., use of tokens/scars); these devices must be motivated within the plot and not be contrived merely to surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought / Argument (Dianoia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasoning, themes, and arguments expressed by characters should be consistent, persuasive, and arise naturally from character and circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle distinguishes thought from character and diction: what characters affirm or argue must cohere with the plot's causal logic and contribute to the whole action rather than being extraneous rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction / Expression (Lexis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of words, phrasing, and metrical expression must suit the characters and the kind of poetry; punctuation and placement of pauses affect meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial notes advise careful attention to punctuation (e.g., 'pone punctum post vocem') and to metrical/morphological choices: diction should clarify thought and occasion, not obscure it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melody / Chorus (Melos) and its proper role
rubrics_metrics.description: Musical elements and the chorus must serve the dramatic action, contributing to mood and unity rather than interrupting or supplanting the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary specifies the chorus should defend the action and not interpose acts that break the continuity of the drama; song and choral components should harmonize with the whole and not be mere spectacle or padding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle (Opsis) as subordinate to poetic art
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual or stage effects are contributory but inferior to plot and character in the essence of tragedy; spectacle can amplify but must not substitute for the poetic fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle treats spectacle as an element that affects the senses but is not the proper object of the poet's art; avoid relying on scenic contrivances to carry the work's moral or emotional weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid implausible contrivances and deus ex machina
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolutions should not depend on implausible intrusions (e.g., arbitrary divine appearances) that evade the plot's internal necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes criticize additions (such as gods suddenly appearing to resolve matters or Homeric interpolations) that undermine the tragedy's probability and the audience's sense of causal coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition should be plausibly motivated (tokens, scars, circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Means of recognition (agnitio) — scars, tokens, coincident circumstances — must be credible within the story-world; recognition must arise from probable grounds, not pure contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and editorial glosses show how recognition often follows from signs that an earlier observer could plausibly have overlooked; the technique should preserve verisimilitude and deepen the plot's logical texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Time (Temporal limits for performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle prescribes that the action represented in a tragedy should occur within the span of a single day (the usual practice for Attic tragedy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'Spectandum Aristoteles tradit tempus, quod conſumunt Tragœdiæ... uno die' — performance/time constraints shape the plot's permissible scope; epic can cover longer durations but must still respect unity and magnitude principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (Mimesis) over mere narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and drama are imitations of actions rather than mere narrative reportage; the poet should enact deeds and characters rather than merely tell of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theologizing or explanatory asides that report incidents instead of dramatizing them weaken the work's poetic effect; show the action in deeds and speech to engage audience perception and emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of genre-specific devices and meters
rubrics_metrics.description: Different poetic genres (epic, tragedy, lyric) have appropriate forms, meters, and devices; the poet must observe those conventions while preserving the art's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial notes discuss metrical and lexical variants, and the Poetics distinguishes verbal/musical forms appropriate to each genre; violating formal expectations may impair intelligibility or effect.
